speechtext:
Having given due notice, I rise on a question of privilege which, I believe, affects all members of the house in circumstances which will, once again, indicate the method the government is using to communicate policy to the public.
Yesterday during the question period I asked a question in connection with old age security pension legislation. My question was termed impertinent by the Acting Prime Minister, and there were other remarks made, as has been the case since I began this effort on behalf of the senior citizens of Canada.
In fact, the policy of the government appeared in detail on the front page of the Toronto Star, on November 1,	1966, as
proposed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare who suggested that the legislation would be before the house this month. Allow me to outline, now, the question of privilege which arises in relation to what has taken place as far as members of this house are concerned.
First of all, I raised the question of the possibility of an increase in old age pensions from the federal old age pension fund, on January 19. Since that time the fund has I believe swollen to the sum of $320 million, further proving my point in that regard.

My question of privilege relates to the method by which the government has given details of its legislation to the public before making a statement on the matter in the House of Commons, particularly in the light of what took place during the question period yesterday, e (2:40 p.m.)
I also raised this matter on April 6 of this year as reported at page 3959 of Hansard, as well as on many occasions since that date. Indeed a notice of motion on this subject, which I moved, was discussed at length and talked out by government members. Then we come to the question period on October 21-and I know government members will not like this because it shows the method by which they like to carry on their administration and, so far as that is concerned, deceive the country. On October 21, in relation to a statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) with respect to the sums of money that would be spent on foreign aid in ensuing years, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when legislation would be introduced to increase old age pensions, and the answer he gave on that occasion, as recorded at page 8952 of Hansard, was:
I hope that legislation will be before the house very shortly on that matter.
With reference to the article which appeared in yesterday's Toronto Daily Star I must explain to the house that obviously there is communication between the minister's office and that newspaper, otherwise the story would have appeared in other press media. I believe the minister's executive assistant has a certain nostalgic association with that newspaper, which would give rise
November 2, 1966

Alleged Denial of Press Release to the article which appeared on its front page yesterday. The articles says, without any denying, that the government is now-
-tying the ribbons on its new package, which it hopes to introduce in the Commons this month for delivery to the pensioners starting January 1.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that, my having raised this question first on January 19, 1966, to have this information given to the people of the country in this way is certainly a breach of privilege of the house and of all hon. members. The heading on the article is, "Help for Thousands in Pension Changes Coming Up in the Commons." I do not disagree with such help. I think my efforts on behalf of the senior citizens of Canada are well known, and I think my request to the government at such an early date this year indicates my concern. But since that time we have had nothing but an increase in the cost of living, and these elderly citizens have been denied that small amount of money which would help to serve their needs in present day conditions.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote the article which contains the breach of privilege of which I complain, so that the house will be apprised of the information that has been released without the House of Commons being informed. The article is written by one Perry Anglin, a staff reporter for the Toronto Star, and it reads as follows:
Ottawa-Under a proposed refinement-
It does not refer to any great piece of new legislation.
-in the federal guaranteed income plan for the old age pensioner, a person who now receives a total income of $125 a month, including his $75 old age pension, will receive an extra $5 from the government.
Thousands of Canada's 1,100,000 old age pensioners with an income up to $135 a month are now expected to benefit from the revision.
The original plan has been expected to guarantee pensioners a minimum income of $105 a month- including their basic $75 pension.
Under it, a pensioner whose only income was the basic $75 would get a full $30 extra from the government; any private income he had in addition to the $75 would be deducted from the $30.
But under the refinements proposed by Health Minister MacEachen a sliding scale of reduced benefits will be available to pensioners with a total income up to $135 a month.
For those pensioners, the maximum benefit of $30 under the new plan would be reduced by half the amount of their total income over the basic $75.
If a pensioner's total monthly income is $125, here's how he would receive the extra $5:
Half the amount of the $50 he receives over the basic $75 is $25 and this is subtracted from the $30 maximum benefit to give him $5.

The government is now tying the ribbons on its new package, which it hopes to introduce in the Commons this month for delivery to the pensioners starting January 1.
That, Mr. Speaker, I submit constitutes the breach of privilege which I bring before the house. This game of cat and mouse with the old age pensioners and with parliament must cease. I further suggest that it finally puts the tag on the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. MacEachen) and the cabinet, that what is involved is no longer a needs test but is in fact a means test.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon three of my colleagues and I had a very useful discussion with a delegation from the United Automobile Workers headed by their Canadian director. Among matters discussed were training and retraining programs, but the most time, perhaps, was devoted to the matter previously raised by the hon. member for Ontario and others, namely, the transitional assistance benefit program, commonly known as T.A.B. This is a benefit program for workers, who may be laid-off as a result of readjustments arising from the operation of the Canada-U.S. automobile agreement.
I think members of the house should know that my colleagues and I advised the delegation yesterday that the government had given very careful consideration to the T.A.B. program, and to the representations that they have made on more than one occasion, including the occasion on which the hon. member for Ontario was present with a delegation from Oshawa. We advised these people that the regulations governing this program would be amended in order to permit workers who have used up their supplementary unemployment benefits, commonly known as S.U.B. credits, during lay-offs certified by the adjustment assistance board, to draw them subsequently as transitional assistance benefits. In other words, the effect of this change in regulations would be that T.A.B., the transitional assistance benefit program, will underwrite the S.U.B. program, and the workers will get earned benefits, if needed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Skeena asked a question to which I should like to reply now. The discussions of the steering committee determined a general feeling that trips to Indian reserves would be more productive and comprehensive in the form of a number of small study groups visiting numerous areas rather than the necessarily restricted and formal procedure of the whole committee visiting only a few areas. It is not clear whether the present terms of reference give such authority, and new terms will be sought as soon as possible if required. Travel arrangements will be made thereafter at the convenience of members of the committee. I hope the committee will be able to assemble for that purpose within a matter of a few days.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Batten in the chair:

Mr. Chairman, last night when we adjourned at ten o'clock I think we had pretty well established the position that while the government gives lip service to the principle that parliament is entitled to information-some government spokesmen have even bragged about setting up a committee to ensure that information is made available-this government continues to go to desperate lengths to keep information from parliament. They are so worried about the defence situation that the minister goes to any length to prevent it from coming to light.
I think the house should really examine the position in which the Liberal party has put itself, as evidenced by the vote taken today, so that there should be no question that it is official Liberal party policy today that the government does not answer to parliament. By voting against the motion they have said that it is the government which is supreme and not this house. The minister has said so during the debate. For instance, on page 9346
Interim Supply
of Hansard, when speaking of witnesses before a committee he said;
This does not mean and cannot mean, of course, that departmental officials and serving officers appear before the parliamentary committee as private individuals speaking on their own behalf. They are there as representatives of the department.
Mr. Chairman, to suggest that a parliamentary committee is limited to summoning before it only those witnesses whom the minister decides should come is nonsense.
I did not say that.

There is a suggestion inherent in what he said that if a witness works in the department, then he is a department representative and as such speaks for the minister. We, in this party, reject this contention most emphatically. Everyone who believes in a responsible and democratic government must uphold the power of parliament. When parliament summons witnesses through its committees, whether those witnesses be civil servants or officers of the armed forces, they should be allowed to present whatever facts are in their possession. It should not be up to the minister to decide whether they should do so or not.
The minister emphasized this again on page 9346 of Hansard when he said:
It is fundamental to our parliamentary practice that the minister responsible for a department will have the sole discretion as to the limits of the special material that his officers may present.
Again, it is spelled out very clearly, in the statement: "the minister shall have the whole responsibility as to what material his officers may present." Can there be a clearer statement of the minister's belief in his superiority over parliament?
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I suggest that this is not just a statement of the minister's that can be denied by other ministers, the Prime Minister, or Liberal backbenchers. The motion rejected today by the house, as a result of the Liberals voting against it, emphasizes the principle to which I have alluded. The minister has rejected the question of privilege. As we have seen in the Landymore case, material was deleted. When the minister talked about privilege, he must have been aware what judgment would be made of his remarks to the effect that he had a right to determine what the committee shall hear. Does the minister think that his right is superior to that of parliament? When the minister's party voted today, rejecting the

November 2, 1966
Interim Supply
motion tor production of documents having to do with that question of privilege, the position of the Liberal party was made clear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I must advise the hon. member that he is now reflecting on a decision of the house.

With all respect, Mr. Chairman, I had not intended reflecting on a decision of the house. I was merely pointing out to hon. members opposite the position that their party is in as a result of the vote this afternoon. I must point out that the stand taken by this minister with respect to defence matters was that they shall not be revealed to the House of Commons. I suggest that those so enthusiastically backing this minister, who steadfastly refuses to allow defence matters to see the light of day, have got themselves and their party into a position which would make Sir Wilfrid Laurier turn in his grave, and cause distress to other Liberals walking the streets. I know that my Liberal friends at home will be more than a little annoyed at the Minister of National Defence. Their reaction will be, I am sure, that no matter how embarrassing some of these defence matters may have been to the minister, the embarrassment heretofore is as nothing compared to the embarrassment of the Liberal party now as a result of the vote in the house today. That vote will embarrass the Liberal party and all those who believe in democracy.
The position has been made very clear by the Liberal party that the minister is superior to parliament. That is the official position now. Their position is that they are not responsible to parliament.
Is there no way by which members in this house can reach the minds and consciences of members opposite? Are members opposite going to sit as a solid phalanx, steadfastly refusing to put pressure on that minister to do what everyone knows should be done, namely, giving the facts to parliament so that we can intelligently discuss these pressing matters of defence?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must advise the hon. member that the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, on entering the debate on interim supply for a few moments this afternoon I, too, want to make remarks with respect to defence policy and defence matters. It has been my privilege and honour in the short time I have been in this

house to be a member of the defence commit-tie, and to be one of the original group forming that defence committee when it was established in 1963. So, this has been a matter which I have followed with keen interest, and which 1 will continue to follow with keen interest, particularly when one watches the evolving progress of the integration of our armed forces and the steps leading towards unification.
Today in particular, following the discussions of the last couple of days, I want to allude to a document which has come to hand. I am not referring to that document which showed, side by side, the documents of Admiral Landymore and those of the hon. Minister of National Defence-that Rosetta stone, that Cleopatra's needle from which we can discern and determine not only what was in the mind of the minister but what was in the mind of the navy.
I have another document to which I shall refer in a moment or two. This is a very interesting document prepared by the new defence critic of the Tory party.
Hon. members will remember that on October 31, in the exchange which took place as recorded on page 9353 of Hansard the minister said, in part, addressing the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona:
-did you in fact burn 19 copies of this memorandum because you were afraid it would see the light of day?
I am referring to the study paper, or to the policy paper of the Conservative party on the subject of defence. The hon. member replied:
I don't know what you are talking about and you don't know either.
Then the Minister of National Defence went on to say to the hon. member:
Do you deny such a document exists, that there was in fact a memo prepared by Admiral Brock?
To which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona replied:
I have no idea of such a document.
It was at this time that the hon. member for Halifax entered into the discussion and spilled the beans. He rose, and it was rather comical and said:
My hand lies very deeply in that document and I am very concerned with it.
His hand, at this moment, lies deeply in the other hon. member's back. The hon. member for Halifax went on to say:
The minister talked about drafts that were changed, and one thing and another. The first 19 were destroyed; indeed, the first 19 were burned.
November 2, 1966

Imagine that. That is just like the Nazis during world war II. He continued:
What came cut of it I hope will be presented publicly at the right time to the Canadian people and will represent a viable, reasonable and worthy alternative to the utter nonsense we have listened to over the last 20 minutes. It is a very valid document.
In those words, the hon. member for Halifax announced the defence policy position of the Tory party. He hinted to us that this was the position which would be unveiled, I presume at the oncoming convention which will take place in one week or ten days. At that time the new defence critic of the Tory party would reveal the new position of the Tory party-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
I should be delighted to permit a question.

In reading those statements of mine, is the hon. member suggesting that I was not telling the truth to the house, or that I necessarily went along with everything that the hon. member for Halifax suggested? Is that what the hon. member is saying?
The answer to your question is obvious.

I would not endeavour to make an interpretation of the things set out. I would not do anything like that. I impute no motives to hon. members. I simply say to the hon. member: this is what stands in the record and whatever people in the house are prepared to believe, they will have to decide, I am sure. The hon. member will have to live with those decisions.
I have no trouble living with my stand. If the hon. member wants to make a charge that the situation is other than as I said, then I suggest he should be an hon. member for a change.
I make no charge. I simply read Hansard. Is that an offence in the House of Commons?
Watch out for the leaks.

You can imagine how much interest would be caused if it were known that a paper like that were abroad in the land. What scurrying there would be in the halls of the press gallery if the hon. member for Halifax, still eager to push along with the
Interim Supply
new policy, still seeing himself the wave of the future, went to the press gallery and gave them one of these confidential documents.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I want to read something which will throw light on the nature of this document.
In the Citizen today we find on page 22 a story by John Walker of the Southam News Services describing how the document was taken to the press gallery and unveiled there.
The Conservatives have Anally released Admiral Jeffry Brock's "confidential" national defence policy paper which, in its third revised version, is being studied by the Tory caucus' defence committee.
Would it not be interesting to know who has been revising the admiral's paper?
The secret paper, which calls for a pause in the headlong integration program and for Canada to abandon all nuclear weapons now, was given out by Halifax M.P. J. M. Forrestall. He, along with Edmonton's Terry Nugent, has been leading the present Conservative battle with Defence Minister Hellyer over unification. It was the first time that the Conservatives had admitted that the retired admiral, who was asked to quit in 1964, was drafting defence policy papers for the party.
Indeed, it was the first time that we on this side of the house realized that the hon. member for Calgary North had been replaced as defence adviser of his party; that he was out, and that a new defense adviser had been chosen. This was the first time we knew, for example, that the hon. member for Edmonton West was no longer in the inner conclaves of his party as a defence critic and that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre had been shown the door because a new defence critic was on his way in. It was an interesting revelaton.
A lot better than Lee.

The article goes on:
As late as Monday night, when Mr. Hellyer asked Mr. Nugent in the House what had happened to 19 copies of the second draft-
How many drafts of admirals' papers do you people over there keep writing?
-of this secret document, Mr. Nugent denied knowing about them. A week ago the Edmonton member was trying to get a member of the parliamentary press gallery before the bar of the house for suggesting Admiral Brock was directing his actions from the public gallery.
Oh, oh.

Just a minute; it is funny, but I must control myself.
Mr. Forrestall said that the admiral had been asked to make a study of defence policy "about 18 months ago" by E. A. Goodman, Toronto lawyer and party organizer during the 1965 campaign.

November 2, 1966
Interim Supply
So, 18 months ago a new defence adviser had been quietly contacted by a vice president of the Tory party and asked to work on behalf of the Tories, all unknown to the defence critics on the front bench opposite who have been handing out advice to the minister of defence. Behind them, there was a new apple in the barrel.
"We wanted a reasonable alternative to the present defence policy," said Mr. Forrestall-
I suppose they wanted a reasonable alternative to present Tory defence policy. Not being able to get one which satisfied them from their own front bench, they brought in Admiral Brock. It all becomes quite clear. They wanted an alternative defence policy-
-which could be studied by the defence committee and then perhaps put before the whole caucus as a policy for the party in the next election campaign."
Admitting that a Toronto newspaper had gotten hold of the paper-"I hope it is the right version" -Mr. Forrestall said the committee had decided to release it.
They were not even sure what they were releasing. By his own admission, even the hon. member was not too sure what he was giving to the press gallery with regard to Tory policy. But it was on paper. And he did have it from an admiral, so let it go.
The report goes on:
He said 19 copies of the second version had been burned, to keep them secure. He didn't know where the 20th copy was.
If ever there was a Keystone Cop's comedy going on in the ranks of the Conservatives, it has to be this.
Here is the 20th copy.
You are wrong. I have the 20th copy.
Oh, oh.
Take care that nothing leaks.

I continue to quote:
Admiral Brock, an outspoken opponent of Defence Minister Hellyer's unification plans for the three services, had revised the text three times-
I wonder who was leaning over his shoulder, editorial pen in hand, to help revise this thing.
-the last time being in the past month or so for the reopening of the house when the first attempt was made to get Mr. Hellyer to hold off unification.
Mr. Forrestall said Opposition Leader Diefenbaker had seen the document-he wasn't sure which version-and while not exactly blessing the project, he had encouraged them to continue.

It is a mixed up comedy. He was not sure which version.
Others who had seen the Brock policy statement, he said, included caucus defence committee members Douglas Harkness-
Now, of course, relegated to the background-
-Marcel Lambert-
Another defence critic carefully passed up, though a former vice-chairman of the defence committee-
-Gordon Churchill, Angus MacLean, Heber Smith and Davie Fulton-
The heir apparent
-about 20 to 25 in all. The admiral who has been here following the debates for several weeks and working in the office of one of the Tory members who has been absent-
Imagine that! They had sneaked him into the building, ensconced him in an absent member's room; they had given him virtually everything except a seat in the House of Commons. And the new Dauphin, the new prince, was upstairs in his chamber ready to be brought down.
Trinity will soon be vacant.

What a story! Well, this new defence critic-
-has seen Mr. Diefenbaker and talked to Mr. Nugent on a number of occasions before his recent attacks on the government.
He had talked to Mr. Nugent. Mr. Nugent had talked to him. Now, here is a curious thing about the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona. I am imputing no motive when I say to him that here was this hon. member surrounded by 20 people, all with editorial pens in their hands and all of them furiously editing the work of this admiral ensconced in his room upstairs. All of those people were coming in from time to time and saying: "Have you got the paper ready? We need it for the Tory convention."
He was there and day after day we had to listen as the hon. member rose to give us one more instalment of Terry and the Pirates, and his life with Paul Hellyer.
Oh, oh.

The amazing thing about
all this was that he did not have the slightest idea, not a clue, as to what was going on upstairs.
November 2, 1966

On a question of privilege; I hate to spoil an entertaining speech, but if the hon. member wants to refer to what I said in the house he should not use the old Liberal trick of misinterpreting, distorting and twisting my words. The question asked of me referred to these copies being burned. I had some idea that people were making submissions, but when the minister talks about all these things being burned I do not know what he is referring to. If the hon. member would refer to what I said, instead of what he would like me to have said, I would have no objection.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, the last remarks of the hon. member I think should be withdrawn. He said "so slyly", imputing an improper motive, I suggest, or an improper method of doing business. The entire tenor of the speech of the member I suggest, when compared to an honourable way of putting

We only have to look at the way he handled this document, his misrepresentation of it to the house, and his refusal to answer questions about it or to identify it. Even then, when a document is being read, he does what no other member in this house would have the nerve to do; he pretends to be reading it and leaves out the part of it which would identify it. I suggest this is the type of activity he has been carrying out, instead of defending his minister and explaining things. If he wanted to carry out an attack on me, this has been a very fine and fanciful performance with no regard for any decency in respect of a member of this house.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to follow the line which has been taken by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. I am not particularly concerned whether the Conservatives have policy papers,-whether they burn them, chew them up, or swallow them. I do not think this is a matter of great national moment. I do wish to say, however, a few words about the agreement which was tabled in the House of Commons last Friday by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with reference to permission for Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to build a line through the United States from Emerson, Manitoba to Sarnia, Ontario. I should like to express the concern which this party feels in respect of the policy decision which is involved in this.
On August 25 the Prime Minister publicly gave the reason the government had decided to reject the application of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines to build this line through the United States.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
They were good and sufficient reasons, reasons which in my opinion still stand. On October 4 the Prime Minister issued another statement saying that the cabinet had reversed itself, and that in view of the fact Trans-Canada had made certain changes in its application permission was being granted to build this line. The minister has now tabled the agreement and we have had a chance to see it. Yesterday, he endeavoured to make some defence of the decision.
This pipe line is an important matter to the people of Ontario and Quebec who will be served with natural gas from that line, but that is only part of a wider picture. It is part
November 2, 196G

of a much greater problem which the people of Canada must face. Yesterday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources quoted that old saying, that the art of governing is the art of foreseeing and choosing. He said the government had to make a choice in respect of this application by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines.
Let me submit to the committee that the choice with reference to the location of the pipe line is only part of a much wider choice which the government is making and which the Canadian people must make. That choice is whether or not Canada is going to survive as an independent nation with an autonomous economy over which its people have complete control. We have to decide whether this country is going to be a nation full, free and independent or whether we are going to become part of a great economic hegemony on the North American continent.
When I pose this choice, it is not because I am anti-American as some newspapers have suggested. As a matter of fact, while I differ with the policies of the United States government on a number of matters, I have a great regard for the citizens of that country. I took some of my education in the United States and I have members of my family who live in the United States and who are citizens of that country. I have had the privilege of lecturing from time to time in a number of United States universities and I presume, if for some reason or other I were not able to live in Canada, I would probably choose to live there because I like that country and its citizens.
But I also happen to be one of those individuals who believes that this country has something worth preserving and that this country has a contribution to make to the world which it cannot make if it is merged into the United States hegemony. I intend to use all the influence I can wield to see to it that in the choice which the Canadian people must make in the next few years we, come down not on the side of continentalism but on the side of a sane national policy to keep Canadian national identity and to develop a people who are strong and free.
This is a choice which I think must be made by the Canadian people in the next few years, because in my opinion we do not have unlimited time, the sands of time are running out. My criticism of the government is that it is already making a choice as a result of which we are witnessing in this country a creeping continentalism, and bit by bit the resources and the economic facilities of this

nation are coming increasingly under the control of foreign investors.
Canada is a country in which over 70 per cent of its oil producing and refining industry, over 60 per cent of its mining industry, over 54 per cent of its manufacturing industry, 90 per cent of its automobile industry and 100 per cent of its aircraft manufacturing industry, is entirely in the hands of foreign investors. Foreign control has now moved into our financial institutions, into insurance and into advertising agencies so that more and more control today is in the hands of foreign investors and less and less of the decision making power lies with Canadian citizens.
The hon. member for Davenport, the former minister of finance, made a speech which was reported in the Globe and Mail of October 26 of this year. That article reads in part as follows:
Former finance minister Walter Gordon said yesterday that the Canadian economy has fallen so far under foreign control that professional persons have become fearful about expressing opposition to the trend.
The article quotes him as saying:
'It means that lawyers and accountants, engineers and geologists, many advertising and insurance agents, and people in all phases of finance, are hesitant to speak publicly about their fears of what is happening to Canada.'
The article then states:
He suggested this situation would continue until Canada, like Mexico, establishes clear rules and regulations respecting foreign ownership and control of domestic businesses and resources.
The article then goes on to say:
Mr. Gordon noted that the Liberal conference had approved a resolution in favour of North American free trade. This resolution, if implemented, he said, would almost certainly result in some kind of merger with the United States.
The actions of this government over the past two years have caused concern to the people who are devoted to the idea of maintaining a national Canadian identity. We have the Columbia river agreement by which we turned over to the control of United States investors and power companies one of the largest rivers on this continent. The Cana-dian-U.S. auto agreement, about which great things were predicted but which today really means that three large automobile companies, entirely owned and operated from the United States, have a privilege which is denied any Canadian citizen or company, that is, the right to move their cars freely back and forth across the border without paying duty. As it

now transpires, this agreement gives these companies the right to move European cars into Canada free of duty.
We all know about the recent conference the Liberal party held in the city of Ottawa. At that conference the member for Davenport, and some of the holdouts from the Kingston and Peterborough conferences, endeavoured to put up a fight for maintaining some semblance of Canadian nationalism, but apparently they were completely routed. Apparently the continentialists in the Liberal party were triumphant.

I think the most significant remark came from a delegate from the government of Saskatchewan who said that as far as foreign investment is concerned, all we want is more of it.
Now we have this agreement, which by itself may not excite the public. However, as part of the total picture, it is just another step in this program of continentalism by which the government is seeking to build a great economic complex in which Canada will be only a small part and Canadian decisionmaking power will be infinitesimal. All history has demonstrated that political power always follows economic power. We have to make up our mind whether we who inherited an independent northern nation are going to pass that on to our children, or whether we are going to look forward to the day when they will be part of this great, northern, rationalized economic hegemony under which all the things that Canada represents will have disappeared.
I am not arguing that there may not be advantages in an economic merger, and ultimately a political merger, with the United States. Of course there are some advantages. But I believe there are great disadvantages. I think there are both tangible and intangible assets that are worth preserving in the Canadian way of life. It is because I believe this that I am so critical of this agreement which has been placed before the house by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
The moment anyone opposes continentalism he is accused, as the hon. member for Davenport was accused at the recent Liberal conference here in Ottawa, of being a protectionist, of trying to make Canada an isolated national unit. This is not the case. I recognize, as I am sure every person who has studied the problem does, that as President Kennedy once said of the United States and

Canada, geography has made us neighbours and history has made us friends. Because we are side by side with the most powerful industrial nation in the world, it is only natural that the United States will be our best customer and that we will be her best customer. I hope that will always continue to be the case.
We do not oppose exporting goods to the United States; of course not. We do not oppose exporting fuels such as gas, oil and coal to the United States. But we believe there must be a prior claim for Canadian industry and development. We believe that if there are surpluses which we do not require, of course we should be prepared to sell them to the United States. But our first consideration must be for the utilization of those assets which can help to develop this country.
The other day someone said-I think it was the hon. member for Bow River-that if you can sell wheat to communist countries, why cannot you sell gas to the United States? There is a great deal of difference between selling wheat and gas. You can grow a fresh crop of wheat each year, but there is a limit to how much gas we have. Therefore we should make sure that before we export any fuel or any form of energy we retain sufficient to promote our own economic growth.
There is a great deal of difference between trading with a nation and allowing a nation to take over the control of our economy. The Prime Minister spoke on this subject the other day, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of October 31. Over the week end the Prime Minister addressed the Quebec wing of the Liberal Federation of Canada in Montreal, and is quoted as having said:
Canada could not seriously contemplate a free trade union with the United States and the Caribbean countries unless the Canadian economy were strong enough and Canadian ownership and control of all our sources of prosperity complete enough to ensure that we could not lose our political independence.
That sums it up very well. Of course we want to trade with the United States. Of course we want to do business with them or anyone else. But the paramount issue is that we must be strong enough and must have sufficient ownership and control over our resources to make sure that our economic and political independence are not jeopardized. The interesting thing about the Prime Minister's statement is that, while it is 100 per cent accurate, what the Prime Minister says and what his government does are completely at variance. The Prime Minister stands at the

front door singing, "O Canada, We stand on guard for thee", while at the back door he is selling Canadian resources which are vital and essential to our future development.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this interim supply motion I could not ask for a better introduction to my remarks than those made by the hon. member who has just spoken. There is no issue in Canada today more important than this traditional issue of whether we are going to maintain on the north half of this continent a country that is peculiarly our own. That issue has narrowed down now, after the Liberal meeting in Ottawa two weeks ago, and the remarks by the leader of the New Democratic Party to two words: nationalism and continentalism.
It is clear that the majority of the Liberal delegates meeting at Ottawa in annual convention have turned down the nationalistic proposals of the hon. member for Davenport. We can only take the resolutions which have been passed as an indication of where the Liberal party is heading.
Traditionally, in Canada, the one big distinction between the Liberal party and the Conservative party was in our party's attitude vis-a-vis the United States. We may have many differences, and many things in common, but there is one thing on which there is no equivocation, one thing from which the Conservative party has never deviated. I refer to the attempt to preserve on the north half of the continent a culture and nationalism distinctly our own. We are not trying to say that our culture is different, or that our nationalism is different from any other. We are saying that it is our own, and that is the key issue.
Over and over again in our political and economic history, the Liberal party has gone back to the recurring theme that it is inevitable that we join the United States, and therefore we ought to make it easier instead of more difficult. The history books of this country are full of this.
It is only 190 years ago, Mr. Chairman, that signs were posted on every doorway in the little community of Montreal asking the people to join the democratic nations of the south in rebellion against the crown. The elite of Montreal, both English and French speaking, were for this idea of joining with 23033-599

the democratic people in the colossus to the south. When the chips were down, it was the rank and file French Canadians who resisted this, and the congressionalists were turned back. That was 190 years ago, almost to one week.
I pointed this out because this issue recurs in Canada every generation. I do not want to use my 30 minutes in a recital of this recurring attack on our nationalism and independence. What the hon. member for Davenport has been saying, what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has been saying, is of great concern not only to men in the Liberal party and in the New Democratic Party, but is a vital matter of life and death to every Conservative in this country who deserves to carry the title "Conservative". If we have stood for one thing, it is for our independence.
We now have a weak government, a wrong way government, that seems to make blunders with every move at the local level. This government has allowed itself to be swept along by these Canadian Barry Goldwaters from western Canada into the idea that we have to run pell mell into the arms of the United States colossus. This issue is the key issue in Canada today.
The hon. member who has spoken is a nationalist. I am a nationalist, too, but there is a difference. All during Conservative history we have fought, by restrictive techniques, to give what bargaining power we can to our farmers, our workingmen and our industrialists. This policy has built the base of agriculture, mining and industry in this country. The Conservative party has changed, but in one respect only. This change started years ago, in the Port Hope conference of 1942. Conservatives from Toronto began to express doubts about the efficacy of the high, protective-tariff techniques of defending our nationhood. They pointed out how, under this high barrier, we were inducing companies, mostly foreign owned, to set up here. Those companies wanted the barriers kept. These barriers were one of the biggest inducements to bring ownership of our companies into the hands of foreigners.
So, in the convention of 1942 in Winnipeg, we moved our ideas toward freer trade. There was no sell out of industry, of the farmers or the workingmen. We said: "Let us see our way to joining the world." There was another fundamental reason impelling our thinking, and it was this: the thing that gives us the tremendous living standard that we

However, that is not my point. My point is that modern corporate capitalism is no longer national. It is no longer continental. It is world-wide, and it is becoming increasingly universal. Our labour unions are no longer national, no longer continental; they must reach out and become international, too, as the world moves on, not toward high protective barriers but toward universality. All institutions must be in tune with this movement or they are not serving their people well.
Modern nationalism is just as strong and it has the same objectives, but there is one difference. We are trying to put our country in tune with the tremendously constructive forces of that phenomenon of our age, international modern capitalism, and we are trying to harness those forces for the national good.
I suppose we could build a wall around our country and try to live within it. That is the natural result of the reactionary policy of hon. members on my left. On the other hand, we could take a chance and, through the efforts of our working people, our business people, our farmers, lumbermen and miners, enter into world-wide competition with every high wage country in the world and every low wage country, and survive.
We, as a government, took that course in 1960. It was a time of recession and we decided that instead of using restrictive techniques we would ask the Canadian people to go out and see not only the basic products of our forests, our farms and our mines, but the products of secondary industry as well. And that policy resulted in the increase of our exports from $4 billion a year to over $10

billion a year. Assistance was given in the form of export credits, by changing the value of the dollar to a realistic figure. We demonstrated that we could succeed.
I stand here as a nationalist, but as an expansionist nationalist. I stand as an opponent of old fashioned restriction, of trying to protect ourselves behind walls, whether in Quebec, in Canada as a whole, or any other restrictive block. I am asking the Canadian people to join the world. There are humane reasons for doing so. There are selfish reasons. But they all add up to the same thing, expansion at home and expansion abroad. This is where I differ from the hon. member for Davenport, and this is where I differ from my hon. friend who sits near me, on this question of seeking to protect the Canadian people.
We differ as to the technique. I think his technique is 60 years out of date. As he points out, all this has a bearing on the pipe line question which we have been considering. I should like to ask him as a favour, as an old friend of mine, to listen to what I believe to be a true description of the situation. I will begin by reminding him of some things we have in common. In 1955, in Saskatchewan I proposed publicly that the price of natural gas in the city of Saskatoon be lowered by 25 per cent from the price at that time, which was 96 cents per 1,000 cubic feet. I argued that if the price were reduced to this extent, the volume of gas purchased by consumers would be so much greater that a greater profit would be made by the power corporation owned and controlled by the government.
At first, there was laughter. But the government changed. I believe the argument which I presented had merit, and a month later the price was reduced from 96 cents to 72 cents. This was not all. The head of the corporation told me that prices were to be reduced again because the government was following a policy of limiting the profit.
This follows because the gas industry is a fixed cost industry; if you increase the volume passing through the pipe line, unit cost is reduced. The consumers benefit, the power corporation benefits, and the whole economy is able to develop. These are historical facts from the province of Saskatchewan and they prove the principle that the industry must have volume.
The second example is also from Saskatchewan. During the time Trans-Canada Pipe Lines was trying to get markets lined up so

that it could obtain financing, the company told the government of Saskatchewan, through the power corporation, that the wholesale price to the public "at the gate" was 26 cents per 1,000 cubic feet. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken was premier of the province. I think he will remember that what saved Saskatchewan was the fact that there are three small gas fields on the border between Saskatchewan and Alberta. By bringing this gas in and placing it into the storage wells in the western part of Saskatchewan, we put another economic factor to work which reduced the price at Regina from 26 cents to 20 cents.
This second factor is the key to the present situation. The operation of pipe line companies in connection with storage are largely dependent on ability to store gas close to the market during the summer season so that it can be brought into consumption in the fall. This increases the load percentage which, in turn, results in a lowering of cost. Anyone who reads this application carefully will find this is the key to the presentation.
I am in a position, today, where I have to be outspoken and I am bound to say that Trans-Canada Pipe Lines has probably been the most stupid company in the economic history of Canada when it comes to presenting a case. It dealt only with the government. It did not have the courtesy to keep the various parties in the opposition informed, including the New Democratic Party, the Social Credit party and the Creditistes. They did not tell the people.
When a monopoly has been given to a private company, the only course open to it if its operations are sound, is to tell the people. The company did not do this and, in a way, it deserves what it is getting here today. In the second place, the National Energy Board is not free from blame. Under the act, the board is responsible for telling the company and for telling the people of Canada what should be done to ensure that gas is available to Canadians. But the crux of this situation is that neither the company nor the energy board gave warning that the consumption of gas in Ontario and Quebec had risen to such an extent in the past five years that the producers were caught in a desperate position two years ago. They realized that if they did not get a line built by November, 1967, they would lose the market in the Windsor area and in the Toronto-Hamilton area to American pipe lines.

But then this uproar developed, not in Canada but in the United States. If hon. members go back and read Hansard of March 1 and March 2 they will find that I asked the Minister of Finance if he would not ask cabinet ministers in the United States government to do something about the fact that our sovereignty was being infringed. If the Americans want to deliver trucks full of goods up to Alaska through our country, we don't trouble them all the way along. We help them, as a good neighbour should. But when western Canadians want to move their gas to their fellow Canadians in Ontario, with 90 per cent of it going right through and the pipe line to be built in one year, from where do we get the opposition? It comes from the American mine workers and from the National Coal Association of the United States. I never thought it would come from Canadians.
I am a nationalist. I do not want to see a Canadian market lost to American pipe lines just because we have not been smart enough to build our own pipe lines fast enough. What makes the southern line economically so attractive? There are two reasons. The first is the tremendous volume that can be moved through it because of the size of the pipe line. But the big factor is that this route has access to storage in western Ontario that the alternative northern route has not got.
Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited has looked at every hole in the ground in northern Ontario to store gas. The way it can reduce the cost is to store gas during the

summer time and then pipe it on to the consumer in the winter time. The company has looked at the mining area of Sudbury. It has looked at every hole possible, but storage must take place where there is impervious rock because the company does not want to lose the gas.
However, there are empty gas holes in southern Ontario. I simply point out that by making use of these storage facilities, one on the Canadian side at Dawn township near Sarnia, and two on the Michigan side, this pipe line company can reduce the price of gas at Windsor and in the whole Union Gas area. The proposal is to put a Canadian gas line through southwestern Ontario, a main trunk line where there is not one now, and then move the gas to Montreal and Toronto.
